entry_json.definition: to say or do something that makes someone feel upset, hurt or insulted
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Humour that works at home can easily offend people from another culture.
example_sentences: I hope I didn't offend her by turning the invitation down.
Advertisers have to be careful not to offend the audiences they depend on.

contexts.text: Humour that works at home can easily offend people from another culture.
I didn't mean to offend anyone, but I do think the rule is unfair.
The study asked whether such images offend religious sensibilities.

confusables.difference: Insult is deliberate and direct: you choose the words to wound. Offend is about the effect, and it is often accidental.
minimal_pair: He offended me without meaning to.

confusables.difference: Annoy is mild irritation about behaviour; offend touches dignity, beliefs or identity.

entry_json.avoid: Do not say "I am offend". The person is offended and the remark is offensive.

entry_json.definition: extremely rude or unpleasant, in a way that hurts or insults people
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Language that was common thirty years ago is now considered offensive.
example_sentences: Several viewers complained that the joke was offensive.
Social media companies are expected to remove offensive content quickly.

contexts.text: Language that was common thirty years ago is now considered offensive.
Personally, I found the advert quite offensive, and I wasn't the only one.
Platforms are under growing pressure to remove offensive material within hours.

confusables.difference: Rude is bad manners in an ordinary situation. Offensive is stronger and usually involves race, religion, gender or something a person cannot change.
minimal_pair: The comment about her religion was offensive.

confusables.difference: Aggressive describes threatening behaviour; offensive describes words or images that insult.

entry_json.avoid: In sport and the military 'offensive' means attacking, not insulting. Context decides the meaning.

entry_json.definition: agreed to or arranged by people in authority, and therefore accepted as correct
entry_json.own_context_sentence: According to official figures, unemployment fell slightly last year.
example_sentences: You need an official translation of your degree certificate.
The official language of the country is Portuguese.

contexts.text: According to official figures, unemployment fell slightly last year.
I'm still waiting for the official result of my exam.
The ministry has not yet issued an official statement on the proposal.

confusables.difference: Official means it comes from an authority. Formal is about style and manners. An official letter is usually formal, but a formal dinner is not official.
Officer is a person; official as an adjective describes a thing. As a noun, an official is someone in a position of authority.

entry_json.avoid: Do not use 'official' to mean 'certain'. Say 'It is confirmed', not 'It is official' in an essay.

entry_json.definition: no longer modern, and belonging to a style or way of thinking from the past
entry_json.own_context_sentence: My parents' views on marriage are quite old-fashioned.
example_sentences: The hotel was a bit old-fashioned, but the staff were lovely.
Some people still prefer old-fashioned paper maps to phone apps.

contexts.text: My parents' views on marriage are quite old-fashioned.
Critics dismiss the policy as old-fashioned, but it has worked for decades.
Younger consumers see printed catalogues as old-fashioned and wasteful.

confusables.difference: Traditional is neutral or positive and respects the past. Old-fashioned usually sounds negative, as if something should have changed.
minimal_pair: It is a traditional wedding ceremony.
His attitude to women is old-fashioned.

confusables.difference: Ancient means thousands of years old. Old-fashioned means merely out of date.

entry_json.avoid: Keep the hyphen. 'Old fashioned' as two words is a spelling error in writing.

entry_json.definition: a space or hole that something can pass through, or the beginning of something
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Light came in through a narrow opening in the roof.
example_sentences: The opening of the film sets up everything that follows.
A small opening in the fence was enough for the animals to escape.

contexts.text: Light came in through a narrow opening in the roof.
We got there late and missed the opening of the concert.
The opening paragraph should state the writer's position clearly.

confusables.difference: Beginning is only about time. Opening can be a physical gap as well as a start, and it is the natural word for a film, a book or a ceremony.
For a free job position, British English prefers vacancy; opening in that sense sounds American.

entry_json.avoid: 'An opening' for a job is American English. In IELTS writing use 'a vacancy' or 'a post'.

entry_json.definition: to work or function, or to control a machine or a business so that it works
entry_json.own_context_sentence: The factory operates twenty-four hours a day.
example_sentences: Only trained staff are allowed to operate the machinery.
The company operates in more than forty countries.

contexts.text: The factory operates twenty-four hours a day.
I've never actually operated a drone, but I'd love to try.
Low-cost airlines operate on very narrow profit margins.

confusables.difference: Work is the everyday word for a machine functioning. Operate is more formal and is also used for running a business or a service.
minimal_pair: The service operates only at weekends.

confusables.difference: Without 'on', operate means run or control. With 'on', it means perform surgery.

entry_json.avoid: Say 'operate on a patient', not 'operate a patient'. Dropping 'on' changes the meaning completely.

entry_json.definition: a medical procedure in which a surgeon cuts into the body, or an organised activity involving many people
entry_json.own_context_sentence: She had an operation on her knee and was back at work in a month.
example_sentences: The rescue operation lasted three days.
The new rules will come into operation next April.

contexts.text: She had an operation on her knee and was back at work in a month.
The rescue operation involved more than two hundred volunteers.
The regulations will come into operation at the start of the financial year.

confusables.difference: Surgery is uncountable and names the field or the practice. An operation is one countable event.
A process happens over time by stages; an operation is organised and directed by people.

entry_json.avoid: Use 'have an operation', not 'do an operation', when you are the patient. The surgeon performs it.

entry_json.definition: a person who competes against you, or who disagrees with a plan or an idea
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Opponents of the scheme argue that it will destroy local businesses.
example_sentences: She beat a much stronger opponent in the final.
The bill has powerful opponents in parliament.

contexts.text: Opponents of the scheme argue that it will destroy local businesses.
My opponent in the semi-final was about a foot taller than me.
Opponents of nuclear power point to the cost of storing waste safely.

confusables.difference: An enemy wants to harm you. An opponent simply takes the other side in a game, an election or a debate.
A competitor is trying to win the same prize or market. An opponent is directly against you in the same contest.

entry_json.avoid: 'Opponent of' is the fixed pattern, not 'opponent against'.

entry_json.definition: to disagree strongly with a plan or policy and try to prevent it
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Local residents strongly oppose the building of a new runway.
example_sentences: Many teachers oppose the return of formal testing for young children.
The union opposed the changes to working hours.

contexts.text: Local residents strongly oppose the building of a new runway.
A lot of people I know oppose the idea, mainly because of the cost.
Economists who oppose the tax argue that it penalises the poorest households.

confusables.difference: Object to is the spoken, everyday version and needs 'to'. Oppose is transitive and more formal.
Refuse is about saying no to something offered to you; oppose is about campaigning against something in general.

entry_json.avoid: Never write 'oppose to' + noun. It is 'oppose the plan' or 'be opposed to the plan'.

entry_json.definition: strongly against something; also used in the phrase 'as opposed to' to contrast two things
entry_json.own_context_sentence: I am strongly opposed to lowering the voting age.
example_sentences: She is opposed to any form of animal testing.
The survey measured spending on public transport as opposed to roads.

contexts.text: I am strongly opposed to lowering the voting age.
I'm not opposed to homework in principle, just to the amount of it.
The chart compares rail use as opposed to car use over a twenty-year period.

confusables.difference: Against is shorter and works in speech. 'Be opposed to' is the formal essay version and sounds stronger.
As a fixed phrase this means 'rather than' and introduces a contrast; it has nothing to do with disagreeing.

entry_json.avoid: 'Opposed to' is followed by a noun or -ing, never by an infinitive: 'opposed to building', not 'opposed to build'.

entry_json.definition: strong disagreement with a plan, or the main political party that is not in power
entry_json.own_context_sentence: The proposal met fierce opposition from local farmers.
example_sentences: There was considerable opposition to the new charges.
The opposition has promised to reverse the decision if it wins.

contexts.text: The proposal met fierce opposition from local farmers.
There was a lot of opposition in my street when they put the parking charges up.
Opposition to the reform came mainly from older voters.

confusables.difference: An objection is one specific reason given against something. Opposition is the general resistance, and is usually uncountable.
Competition is rivalry for a prize or a market; opposition is resistance to a plan.

entry_json.avoid: The pattern is 'opposition to', never 'opposition against'.

entry_json.definition: a part of the body with a particular function, such as the heart or the liver
entry_json.own_context_sentence: The liver is the only organ that can regrow damaged tissue.
example_sentences: Thousands of patients are waiting for an organ transplant.
Smoking damages almost every organ in the body.

contexts.text: The liver is the only organ that can regrow damaged tissue.
My grandfather is on the organ donor register, which I think is admirable.
Shortages of donated organs remain the main obstacle to treatment.

confusables.difference: An organism is a whole living thing. An organ is one part inside it.
minimal_pair: The heart is a vital organ.

confusables.difference: The same spelling names a large keyboard instrument found in churches. Only context separates them.

entry_json.avoid: Do not confuse with 'organisation'. They look similar but share no meaning in modern use.

entry_json.definition: able to plan your work and your time well, or arranged in a careful, ordered way
entry_json.own_context_sentence: You have to be extremely organized to work and study at the same time.
example_sentences: My sister is far more organized than I am.
The conference was well organized and ran exactly to time.

contexts.text: You have to be extremely organized to work and study at the same time.
The event was well organized, with clear signs and enough staff.
Organized crime accounts for a small but costly share of offences.

confusables.difference: Tidy describes a room or a desk. Organized describes a system, a plan or a person's habits.
British English usually spells it 'organised'; both spellings are accepted in IELTS as long as you stay consistent.

entry_json.avoid: Choose one spelling, -ized or -ised, and keep it throughout the whole answer.

entry_json.definition: a person or group that plans and arranges an event
entry_json.own_context_sentence: The organizers expect around five thousand people to attend.
example_sentences: I emailed the organizers to ask about wheelchair access.
Festival organizers had to cancel because of the weather.

contexts.text: The organizers expect around five thousand people to attend.
I was one of the organizers of our school's charity run last year.
I am writing to the organizers to request a refund for the cancelled session.

confusables.difference: An organization is a company or institution. An organizer is the person doing the arranging.
A manager runs something continuously; an organizer sets up one particular event.

entry_json.avoid: Spell it consistently with 'organized'. Do not mix 'organiser' and 'organized' in one answer.

entry_json.definition: the point or place where something begins, or where a person's family comes from
entry_json.own_context_sentence: The origin of the tradition is still disputed by historians.
example_sentences: Many English words are Latin in origin.
The report traces the origins of the crisis to the 1990s.

contexts.text: The origin of the tradition is still disputed by historians.
My family is of Tamil origin, though I was born in London.
Labels must state the country of origin of every ingredient.

confusables.difference: A source is where something is obtained from now: a source of income, a source of data. An origin is where it first came from.
Beginning is a point in time in a story or process. Origin explains where something came from and why.

entry_json.avoid: Use 'of' after origin: 'the origin of the problem', not 'the origin from the problem'.

entry_json.definition: in the beginning, before things changed
entry_json.own_context_sentence: The building was originally a railway station.
example_sentences: I originally planned to study medicine, but I switched to engineering.
The festival was originally held in summer.

contexts.text: The building was originally a railway station.
I'm originally from a small town near the coast.
The scheme was originally intended to last three years.

confusables.difference: Firstly orders points in an argument. Originally orders events in time and implies a later change.
At first is the spoken equivalent and usually contrasts with 'but later'. Originally is neutral and slightly more formal.

entry_json.avoid: 'I am originally from X' is natural; 'I am original from X' is a common error.

entry_json.definition: used to say what will happen if something is not done; also 'in other respects'
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Book early, otherwise you will pay almost double.
example_sentences: The traffic was terrible, but otherwise the journey was fine.
Unless stated otherwise, all figures are in euros.

contexts.text: Book early, otherwise you will pay almost double.
Governments must act now; otherwise the cost of adaptation will rise sharply.
The room was a little small, but otherwise the accommodation was excellent.

confusables.difference: Or else is the informal spoken version of the warning meaning; otherwise is safe in writing.
minimal_pair: Hurry up, or else we'll be late.
Leave now, otherwise you will miss it.

confusables.difference: However contrasts two statements. Otherwise states the consequence of not doing something.

entry_json.avoid: Otherwise joins two sentences, so use a semicolon or a full stop before it, not a bare comma.

entry_json.definition: the one or ones that belong to us
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Their garden is much bigger than ours.
example_sentences: That car isn't ours; ours is the blue one.
The decision is not ours to make.

contexts.text: Their garden is much bigger than ours.
A friend of ours recommended the hotel to us.
The responsibility is ours, not the next generation's.

confusables.difference: Our comes before a noun: our house. Ours replaces the noun completely: this house is ours.
'Our's' does not exist. Possessive pronouns never take an apostrophe.

entry_json.avoid: Never write 'our's'. The correct form has no apostrophe.

entry_json.definition: the final result of a process, meeting or event
entry_json.own_context_sentence: The outcome of the negotiations will affect thousands of workers.
example_sentences: Nobody could predict the outcome of the election.
Early treatment leads to much better outcomes for patients.

contexts.text: The outcome of the negotiations will affect thousands of workers.
Whatever the outcome, I'll be glad the exam is over.
Early intervention is associated with significantly better health outcomes.

confusables.difference: Result is the plain word and is used for scores and figures. Outcome suits a situation whose end was uncertain, and is preferred in academic writing.
A consequence is what follows on afterwards, often bad. An outcome is how the thing itself ended.

entry_json.avoid: Do not say 'outcome result'. Choose one word.

entry_json.definition: used, done or existing outside rather than in a building
entry_json.own_context_sentence: The town has an outdoor pool that opens in June.
example_sentences: Outdoor activities are an important part of the course.
There is an outdoor market every Saturday morning.

contexts.text: The town has an outdoor pool that opens in June.
I much prefer outdoor sports to going to the gym.
Access to outdoor space is strongly linked to mental wellbeing.

confusables.difference: Outdoor is an adjective and goes before a noun. Outdoors is an adverb and goes after the verb.
Outside works as both preposition and adverb; outdoor cannot stand alone after a verb.

entry_json.avoid: Never write 'We played outdoor'. Use 'outdoors' after a verb.

entry_json.definition: outside, not in a building
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Children today spend far less time outdoors than their parents did.
example_sentences: We ate outdoors because the evening was so warm.
In summer the whole class is taught outdoors.

contexts.text: Children today spend far less time outdoors than their parents did.
At weekends I try to be outdoors as much as possible.
Staff who work outdoors need proper protection from the sun.

confusables.difference: Outdoors follows the verb; outdoor sits in front of a noun.
Outside can take an object ('outside the house'); outdoors never can.

entry_json.avoid: Do not write 'outdoors activities'. The adjective is 'outdoor'.

entry_json.definition: on the outside of something, or furthest from the centre
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Rents are much lower in the outer suburbs.
example_sentences: Remove the outer leaves before you cook it.
The outer walls of the castle are still standing.

contexts.text: Rents are much lower in the outer suburbs.
I live in one of the outer districts, so it's about an hour in.
The outer layer of the material keeps the rain out.

confusables.difference: Outer is only an adjective before a noun. Outside is a noun, adjective or preposition.
External is the formal, technical word, often paired with 'internal'. Outer describes physical position.

entry_json.avoid: Outer has no comparative. Do not write 'more outer' or 'outerer'.

entry_json.definition: a short description of the main ideas, without the details; also the shape of something seen from a distance
entry_json.own_context_sentence: The minister gave a broad outline of the new policy.
example_sentences: Write an outline of your essay before you start the first draft.
We could just make out the outline of the mountains.

contexts.text: The minister gave a broad outline of the new policy.
I always write a quick outline before I answer a Task 2 question.
The following section presents an outline of the research method.

confusables.difference: A summary condenses something that already exists. An outline is a skeleton of the main points, often written before the full version.
A draft is a full but unfinished version. An outline is only headings and main points.

entry_json.avoid: 'Outline' as a verb needs no preposition: 'outline the plan', not 'outline about the plan'.

entry_json.definition: considering everything, rather than one particular part
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Overall, the figures show a steady improvement.
example_sentences: Overall, I think the advantages outweigh the drawbacks.
The city has grown overall, although two districts have shrunk.

contexts.text: Overall, the figures show a steady improvement between 2005 and 2020.
Overall, I'd say it was a good decision, even though it was hard at the time.
Overall, the benefits of the scheme appear to justify its cost.

confusables.difference: In general introduces a broad tendency with exceptions. Overall sums up after weighing all the parts, which is why Task 1 overviews use it.
minimal_pair: In general, people prefer cheaper options.

confusables.difference: Total is a number. Overall is a judgement made after considering the numbers.

entry_json.avoid: In an IELTS Task 1 the overview normally starts with 'Overall,' followed by a comma. Do not write 'Overall of'.

entry_json.definition: to have to pay money back to someone, or to feel that you should thank someone for something
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Many graduates owe tens of thousands of pounds in student loans.
example_sentences: I still owe my brother fifty pounds.
She owes her success largely to her parents' support.

contexts.text: Many graduates owe tens of thousands of pounds in student loans.
I owe my parents a lot, honestly, because they paid for everything.
The company still owes its suppliers for goods delivered last year.

confusables.difference: You borrow first; afterwards you owe. Borrow is the action, owe is the state that follows.
Owe and own sound different and mean opposite things: owe is debt, own is possession.

entry_json.avoid: Owe is not used in continuous tenses. Write 'I owe him money', never 'I am owing him money'.

entry_json.definition: the speed at which something happens or at which someone walks or runs
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Technology is changing at a pace that older workers find hard to match.
example_sentences: The pace of life in the capital is exhausting.
She set off at a fast pace and finished first.

contexts.text: Technology is changing at a pace that older workers find hard to match.
The pace of life back home is much slower, which I actually prefer.
Wages have failed to keep pace with rising rents.

confusables.difference: Speed is measurable in numbers. Pace is about how fast something feels or develops, and it collocates with change, life and reform.
Rate is a figure per unit of time: the unemployment rate. Pace is the felt rhythm of a process.

entry_json.avoid: 'Keep pace with' takes 'with'. Do not write 'keep pace to'.

entry_json.definition: something wrapped up to be sent or sold, or a set of things offered together
entry_json.own_context_sentence: The government announced a package of measures to help small businesses.
example_sentences: A package arrived for you this morning.
We booked a package holiday because it worked out cheaper.

contexts.text: The government announced a package of measures to help small businesses.
A package turned up for me this morning and I've no idea what's in it.
I am writing because the package I ordered on 3 May has still not arrived.

confusables.difference: In British English a parcel is what the post delivers. Package is common in American English and in the figurative sense of a set of measures.
A packet is a small paper or plastic bag: a packet of crisps. A package is bigger and usually posted.

entry_json.avoid: Do not say 'a package of information'. Use 'a set of information' or 'a pack'.

entry_json.definition: causing physical pain, or causing sadness and difficulty
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Recovery was slow and painful, but she went back to running.
example_sentences: My knee is still painful when I climb stairs.
Losing the family home was a painful experience.

contexts.text: Recovery was slow and painful, but she went back to running within a year.
My knee's still a bit painful, so I've stopped playing football.
The transition to automation has been painful for older employees.

confusables.difference: Sore is used for a small area that hurts to touch: a sore throat. Painful is broader and stronger, and works for emotions too.
Painless is the opposite and is often used figuratively: a painless process.

entry_json.avoid: Say 'My leg is painful' or 'My leg hurts', not 'I am painful'.

entry_json.definition: light in colour, or with less colour in the face than usual because of illness or shock
entry_json.own_context_sentence: She looked pale and said she had not slept.
example_sentences: The walls were painted a pale green.
He went pale when he heard the news.

contexts.text: She looked pale and said she had not slept for two nights.
The room was a pale yellow, which made it feel bigger.
Prolonged indoor working can leave staff pale and vitamin-deficient.

confusables.difference: Light is neutral for colours. Pale suggests weak or washed-out, and is the only one used about a person's face.
White is a colour; pale describes a lack of colour, so a pale face is not literally white.

entry_json.avoid: For skin, 'pale' describes a temporary look from illness or shock; use 'fair' for someone's natural complexion.

entry_json.definition: a metal container with a handle, used for cooking food on a stove
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Heat a little oil in a large pan before you add the onions.
example_sentences: I burnt the pan and it took an hour to clean.
Use a heavy pan so the rice does not stick.

contexts.text: Heat a little oil in a large pan before you add the onions.
I only really own one decent pan, so I cook fairly simple things.
Cheap pans wear out quickly and are rarely recycled.

confusables.difference: A pot is deep and used for boiling and stews. A pan is shallower and used for frying.
A pane is a sheet of glass in a window. Same sound, no shared meaning.

entry_json.avoid: This word is rarely useful in Task 2. Keep it for Speaking Part 1 or 2 about food and cooking.

entry_json.definition: a group of people chosen to discuss something or make a decision, or a flat piece of material
entry_json.own_context_sentence: A panel of experts reviewed all the applications.
example_sentences: Solar panels now cover most of the roof.
She sat on the interview panel for three days.

contexts.text: A panel of experts reviewed all the applications independently.
There were four people on the interview panel, which was pretty intimidating.
Solar panels have fallen sharply in price over the last decade.

confusables.difference: A committee meets regularly and has ongoing duties. A panel is usually assembled for one purpose, such as judging or interviewing.
A jury decides a court case. A panel judges applications, competitions or debates.

entry_json.avoid: 'On the panel', not 'in the panel', when you mean being a member of it.

entry_json.definition: the group of elected people who make or change a country's laws
entry_json.own_context_sentence: The bill was approved by parliament last month.
example_sentences: Parliament will debate the proposal in October.
She was elected to parliament at the age of thirty.

contexts.text: The bill was approved by parliament after two years of debate.
I honestly couldn't name more than three members of parliament.
Parliament has the final say on how public money is spent.

confusables.difference: The government is the group that runs the country day to day. Parliament is the wider body that makes laws and holds the government to account.
Congress is the equivalent body in the United States; parliament suits the UK and most Commonwealth contexts.

entry_json.avoid: Note the silent middle: it is spelled par-lia-ment, not 'parlament'.

entry_json.definition: a person who takes part in an activity, event or study
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Participants were asked to keep a diary for four weeks.
example_sentences: All participants received a certificate at the end of the course.
Half the participants dropped out before the second stage.

contexts.text: Participants were asked to keep a sleep diary for four weeks.
There were about thirty participants, mostly students like me.
The survey found that regular participants reported lower stress levels.

confusables.difference: A competitor is trying to win. A participant is simply taking part, which is why research reports prefer it.
A member belongs to an organisation over time; a participant takes part in one activity or study.

entry_json.avoid: In academic writing use 'participants' rather than 'subjects', which now sounds outdated.

entry_json.definition: to take part in an activity or event with other people
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Every student is expected to participate in at least one club.
example_sentences: Around two hundred schools participated in the competition.
Older residents are less likely to participate in online consultations.

contexts.text: Every student is expected to participate in at least one extracurricular club.
I participated in a debating competition last year and really enjoyed it.
Employees who participate in training are more likely to stay with the company.

confusables.difference: Take part is the everyday spoken phrase; participate is its formal equivalent and fits an essay better.
minimal_pair: I took part in a race.

confusables.difference: You attend by being present. You participate by doing something active.

entry_json.avoid: Always use 'in': participate in an event. Never 'participate to' or 'participate at'.

entry_json.definition: more than usual, or more than other things; especially
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Housing costs are rising, particularly in the south of the country.
example_sentences: I'm not particularly keen on crowded places.
Air quality is particularly poor during the winter months.

contexts.text: Housing costs are rising, particularly in the south of the country.
I'm not particularly good at cooking, to be honest.
Young graduates are particularly affected by the shortage of affordable housing.

confusables.difference: Almost interchangeable, but 'not particularly' is the natural negative; 'not especially' sounds odd.
Specially means 'for one specific purpose': specially designed. Particularly means 'to an unusual degree'.

entry_json.avoid: Do not begin a sentence with 'Particularly' alone. Attach it to what it modifies, or use 'In particular,'.

entry_json.definition: to some extent but not completely
entry_json.own_context_sentence: The delay was partly caused by bad weather.
example_sentences: I chose the course partly because of its reputation.
The rise in obesity is only partly explained by diet.

contexts.text: The delay was partly caused by bad weather and partly by staff shortages.
I moved here partly for the job and partly because my sister lives nearby.
The fall in sales can be attributed partly to the price increase.

confusables.difference: Partially is more common for physical or technical incompleteness: partially blind, partially built. Partly suits reasons and causes.
Mostly means the larger share; partly means only a share, without saying how big.

entry_json.avoid: 'Partly because' is followed by a clause; 'partly due to' is followed by a noun. Do not mix them.

entry_json.definition: a short section of a book, speech or piece of music, or a narrow way between two places
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Read the passage carefully before you answer the questions.
example_sentences: A narrow passage led from the kitchen to the garden.
The passage of time has softened his opinion.

contexts.text: Read the passage carefully before you answer the questions.
There's a little passage at the back of the building that most people miss.
The passage of time has made the original agreement unworkable.

confusables.difference: An extract is deliberately taken out and reproduced. A passage is any section identified within the whole text.
A corridor is a proper hallway inside a building; a passage is narrower and can be outdoors.

entry_json.avoid: A reading passage is 'a passage', not 'a paragraph'. A paragraph is one block; a passage may hold several.

entry_json.definition: a very strong feeling of enthusiasm for something, or of love
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Photography started as a hobby and turned into a real passion.
example_sentences: She speaks about her subject with genuine passion.
His passion for cycling began at university.

contexts.text: Photography started as a hobby and turned into a real passion.
Teachers who speak with passion are the ones students remember.
A genuine passion for the subject matters more than early ability.

confusables.difference: An interest is mild and can be temporary. A passion is intense and lasting.
minimal_pair: I have an interest in history.
History is a passion of mine.

confusables.difference: A hobby is the activity itself; a passion is the strength of feeling behind it.

entry_json.avoid: The pattern is 'a passion for something', never 'a passion of doing'.

entry_json.definition: a narrow way for walking, or the direction in which something moves or develops
entry_json.own_context_sentence: A path runs along the river all the way to the next village.
example_sentences: Studying part-time was the only realistic path for me.
The storm destroyed everything in its path.

contexts.text: A path runs along the river all the way to the next village.
There's a lovely path near my house that I walk along most evenings.

entry_json.avoid: 'In reality' contrasts with what people believe. Do not use it simply to mean 'actually' in every sentence.

entry_json.definition: fair and sensible, or acceptable in price or amount
entry_json.own_context_sentence: It is reasonable to expect employers to cover the cost of training.
example_sentences: The hotel was clean and the price was reasonable.
A reasonable person would have checked first.

contexts.text: It seems reasonable to expect employers to cover the cost of essential training.
The hotel was clean and the price was very reasonable for the location.
I would be grateful if you could offer a reasonable explanation for the delay.

confusables.difference: Fair is about treating people equally. Reasonable is about being sensible and moderate, and also covers price.
Logical follows from the argument; reasonable also takes practicality and fairness into account.

entry_json.avoid: 'A reasonable amount' means quite a lot, not a small amount. Learners often use it the wrong way round.

entry_json.definition: to remember something, especially when you make an effort to do so
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Participants were asked to recall as many words as they could.
example_sentences: I cannot recall exactly when the change was made.
The manufacturer recalled thousands of vehicles after the fault was found.

contexts.text: Participants were asked to recall as many words from the list as they could.
I can't recall exactly when we moved, but I was about seven.
The manufacturer recalled thousands of vehicles once the fault was identified.

confusables.difference: Remember is the everyday word and can be effortless. Recall implies deliberate effort to retrieve something, and is preferred in research writing.
minimal_pair: I could not recall her name.

confusables.difference: Remind means make someone else remember; recall is something you do yourself.

entry_json.avoid: Recall is not followed by 'to' + verb. Write 'I recall meeting him', not 'I recall to meet him'.

entry_json.definition: a piece of paper showing that goods or money have been received
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Keep the receipt in case you need to return the item.
example_sentences: I've lost the receipt, so they may not refund it.
Please acknowledge receipt of this letter.

contexts.text: Keep the receipt in case you need to return the item within thirty days.
I enclose a copy of the receipt as proof of purchase.
Consumers who retain receipts are significantly more likely to claim refunds.

confusables.difference: An invoice asks for payment before it is made. A receipt proves payment has already happened.
minimal_pair: The invoice is due in 30 days.

confusables.difference: A recipe tells you how to cook something. The two words are often confused because they look alike.

entry_json.avoid: The p is silent: say ri-SEET. Note the spelling ei, not ie.

entry_json.definition: a suggestion that something is good, or advice about the best thing to do
entry_json.own_context_sentence: The report makes six recommendations, only two of which were adopted.
example_sentences: I booked the restaurant on a friend's recommendation.
The committee's recommendation was rejected.

contexts.text: The report makes six recommendations, only two of which have been adopted.
I booked the restaurant on a friend's recommendation and it was excellent.
I would be grateful if you could send a written recommendation to the admissions office.

confusables.difference: A suggestion is one idea offered casually. A recommendation carries authority, from an expert, a report or someone you trust.
A reference in a job application is a letter about your character or work; a recommendation states that something should be done.

entry_json.avoid: 'Make a recommendation', not 'do a recommendation'. Note the double m and single c.

entry_json.definition: to get better after an illness or difficulty, or to get back something that was lost
entry_json.own_context_sentence: The economy took nearly a decade to recover from the crisis.
example_sentences: She recovered fully after six weeks of treatment.
Police recovered most of the stolen equipment.

contexts.text: The regional economy took nearly a decade to recover from the crisis.
I recovered pretty quickly, but I was told to rest for a month.
Police later recovered most of the stolen equipment from a storage unit.

confusables.difference: A doctor or a treatment cures a patient. The patient recovers. The subjects are different.
Improve means get better from any level; recover means return to a previous healthy or normal state.

entry_json.avoid: 'Recover from' something. Do not write 'recover of an illness'.

entry_json.definition: the act of making something smaller or less, or the amount by which it is made less
entry_json.own_context_sentence: There has been a sharp reduction in the number of smokers since 2000.
example_sentences: A reduction in working hours did not reduce output.
Students are entitled to a reduction on rail fares.

contexts.text: There has been a sharp reduction in the number of smokers since 2000.
Students get a reduction on rail fares, which makes a real difference.
A reduction in working hours did not lead to any fall in output.

confusables.difference: Decrease and reduction are close, but reduction suggests someone made it happen, while a decrease can occur on its own.
A discount is money taken off a price for a customer; a reduction is any decrease in amount.

entry_json.avoid: 'A reduction in' the quantity, but 'a reduction of' the amount: a reduction in prices of ten per cent.

entry_json.definition: a mention of something, or a letter about your character written to support an application
entry_json.own_context_sentence: The article makes no reference to the cost of the scheme.
example_sentences: My tutor agreed to write me a reference.
Please quote this reference number in any correspondence.

contexts.text: The article makes no reference at all to the likely cost of the scheme.
My tutor agreed to write me a reference, which was very generous.
With reference to your letter of 3 May, I would like to clarify one point.

confusables.difference: A reference describes what you are like as a worker or student. A recommendation states what should be done.
Mention is the everyday verb; 'make reference to' is the formal noun phrase for the same act.

entry_json.avoid: 'With reference to' opens a formal letter. It is too heavy for the body of an essay.

entry_json.definition: to show or be a sign of something, or to think carefully about something
entry_json.own_context_sentence: The results reflect the amount of preparation each student did.
example_sentences: The figures reflect a change in how the data is collected.
It is worth reflecting on why the policy failed.

contexts.text: The results reflect the amount of preparation each student put in.
Looking back, I reflect on that year as the point where things changed.
The rise in the figures reflects a change in how the data is collected.

confusables.difference: Without 'on', reflect means show or indicate. With 'on', it means think deeply about.
Show presents evidence directly; reflect suggests the thing is a sign of a deeper cause.

entry_json.avoid: Do not write 'reflect about'. The preposition is 'on' or 'upon'.

entry_json.definition: to think of someone or something in a particular way
entry_json.own_context_sentence: The scheme is widely regarded as a failure.
example_sentences: Many people regard homework as a waste of time.
She is regarded as one of the leading researchers in the field.

contexts.text: The scheme is now widely regarded as an expensive failure.
A lot of people I know regard homework as a waste of time.
With regard to your enquiry, I can confirm that places are still available.

confusables.difference: Consider can take an adjective directly: 'consider it unfair'. Regard always needs 'as': 'regard it as unfair'.
'Regards' with an s is a closing in letters, or means 'concerning' in 'as regards'. Keep the two apart.

entry_json.avoid: 'Regard as' is compulsory. 'They regard it a failure' is a common and visible error.

entry_json.definition: relating to one part of a country rather than the whole of it
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Regional differences in income have widened over the last twenty years.
example_sentences: The regional airport handles about two million passengers a year.
There are strong regional accents within a very small area.

contexts.text: Regional differences in income have widened over the last twenty years.
There are really strong regional accents where I'm from, even between nearby towns.
Regional government has responsibility for transport and planning.

confusables.difference: Local means the immediate area around you: a local shop. Regional covers a much larger area within a country.
National covers the whole country; regional is one part of it.

entry_json.avoid: Do not use 'regional' for a small neighbourhood. Use 'local'.

entry_json.definition: to feel sorry about something you have done or failed to do
entry_json.own_context_sentence: I regret not taking the opportunity to study abroad.
example_sentences: We regret to inform you that your application was unsuccessful.
She has never regretted the decision.

contexts.text: I regret not taking the opportunity to study abroad when it was offered.
We regret to inform you that your application has been unsuccessful.
Many graduates later regret choosing a subject purely for its earning potential.

confusables.difference: 'Regret doing' is being sorry about the past. 'Regret to inform' introduces bad news you are about to give.
minimal_pair: I regret to tell you that...

confusables.difference: Apologise is said to the person affected; regret describes your own feeling.

entry_json.avoid: Do not use 'regret to' for past actions. 'I regret to go' does not mean 'I wish I hadn't gone'.

entry_json.definition: at repeated times with roughly equal gaps between them; often
entry_json.own_context_sentence: People who exercise regularly report lower levels of stress.
example_sentences: The bus runs regularly throughout the day.
I regularly check the site for new listings.

contexts.text: People who exercise regularly report significantly lower levels of stress.
I regularly go running at weekends, mainly to clear my head.
The timetable is regularly updated and can be found on the website.

confusables.difference: Often counts how many times. Regularly adds the idea of a repeated pattern at fixed intervals.
Usually describes what normally happens in a situation; regularly describes frequency over time.

entry_json.avoid: Regularly usually sits before the main verb or at the end. Avoid placing it between the verb and its object.

entry_json.definition: an official rule made by a government or organisation
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Tighter regulation of the industry is long overdue.
example_sentences: New safety regulations came into force in January.
The regulations require every landlord to fit smoke alarms.

contexts.text: Tighter regulation of the rental market is long overdue.
There are so many regulations now that small businesses struggle to keep up.
New safety regulations came into force at the start of January.

confusables.difference: A law is passed by parliament. A regulation is a detailed rule made under a law by a government body.
A rule can be made by anyone, including a school or a club. A regulation is official and legally backed.

entry_json.avoid: Uncountable when it means the activity ('regulation of the industry'), countable when it means individual rules ('the regulations say').

entry_json.definition: to refuse to accept an idea, an offer or an application
entry_json.own_context_sentence: The council rejected the proposal for a third time.
example_sentences: My application was rejected without an interview.
The theory has been rejected by most researchers.

contexts.text: The council rejected the proposal for a third time in November.
My application was rejected without even an interview, which stung.
The original theory has since been rejected by most researchers in the field.

confusables.difference: Refuse is about saying no to something offered to you. Reject is deciding that something submitted is not good enough.
Deny is saying something is not true, or not allowing access. Reject is turning something down.

entry_json.avoid: The noun 'a reject' means a faulty product and is offensive when used of a person. Use 'rejection' for the act.

entry_json.definition: to show or have a connection with something, or to understand and sympathise with someone
entry_json.own_context_sentence: The chapter relates directly to what we discussed last week.
example_sentences: Most complaints relate to waiting times rather than treatment.
I can relate to what she went through.

contexts.text: Most complaints relate to waiting times rather than to the quality of treatment.
I can really relate to that, because I went through something similar.
This chapter relates directly to the argument set out in the introduction.

confusables.difference: The same phrase does two jobs: showing a link between things, and understanding a person's feelings. Context decides.
Concern states the subject matter directly and takes no preposition: 'the report concerns housing'.

entry_json.avoid: Relate needs 'to' in almost every use. 'This relates the issue' is not correct English.

entry_json.definition: connected with something, or belonging to the same family
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Stress-related illness accounts for a large share of absence from work.
example_sentences: The two problems are closely related.
Are you related to the woman who runs the shop?

contexts.text: Stress-related illness accounts for a large share of absence from work.
Are you related to the woman who runs the corner shop? You look alike.
The two problems are closely related and cannot be solved separately.

confusables.difference: Related is the adjective meaning connected. A relative is a person in your family.
Relevant means important to the matter in hand. Related only means connected.

entry_json.avoid: Hyphenate compounds: work-related, stress-related, weather-related.

entry_json.definition: the way in which two things are connected, or a member of your family
entry_json.own_context_sentence: There is no clear relation between class size and exam results.
example_sentences: Trade relations between the two countries have improved.
Most of my relations still live in the same town.

contexts.text: There is no clear relation between class size and final exam results.
Most of my relations still live in the same town, so we see each other often.
Trade relations between the two countries have improved since the agreement.

confusables.difference: Relationship is preferred for connections between people. Relation suits abstract links between facts or figures, and 'relations' in the plural means diplomatic or trade links.
minimal_pair: a close relationship with my sister
the relation between income and health

confusables.difference: Relative is the more common word for a family member; relation is slightly more formal in that sense.

entry_json.avoid: 'In relation to' means concerning. Do not use it when you simply mean 'compared with'.

entry_json.definition: a member of your family
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Several relatives travelled from abroad for the wedding.
example_sentences: I have a distant relative who emigrated in the 1950s.
Older people who live near relatives report less loneliness.

contexts.text: Several relatives travelled from abroad for the wedding.
Older people who live close to relatives report significantly less loneliness.
Caring for elderly relatives falls disproportionately on women.

confusables.difference: Both mean a family member, but 'relative' is more common in modern English.
As an adjective, relative means compared with something else: relative poverty.

entry_json.avoid: Do not use 'relative' for a friend. It means family only.

entry_json.definition: to a fairly large or small degree, when compared with something else
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Rents here are relatively low compared with the capital.
example_sentences: The process is relatively straightforward.
Relatively few people take up the offer.

contexts.text: Rents in the area are relatively low compared with those in the capital.
It was relatively easy once someone showed me how.
Relatively few households have taken up the grant since it was introduced.

confusables.difference: Fairly is a simple degree word. Relatively always implies a comparison, stated or understood.
Comparatively is a close synonym and slightly more formal. Both need a point of comparison.

entry_json.avoid: Do not use 'relatively' with no comparison in mind. It should replace 'quite' only when something is being measured against something else.

entry_json.definition: calm and not worried, or informal and without strict rules
entry_json.own_context_sentence: The atmosphere in the office is relaxed but the deadlines are strict.
example_sentences: I felt completely relaxed by the second day of the holiday.
The school has a fairly relaxed attitude to uniform.

contexts.text: The atmosphere in the office is relaxed, although the deadlines are strict.
I felt completely relaxed by about the second day of the holiday.
A relaxed classroom environment has been shown to improve participation.

confusables.difference: Relaxed describes how you feel. Relaxing describes the thing that produces the feeling.
Calm suggests staying steady under pressure. Relaxed suggests there is no pressure to begin with.

entry_json.avoid: Do not say 'The holiday was relaxed'. A holiday is relaxing; a person is relaxed.

entry_json.definition: making you feel calm and free from worry
entry_json.own_context_sentence: A long walk at the end of the day is the most relaxing thing I do.
example_sentences: It was a relaxing weekend with nothing planned.
Some people find cooking relaxing.

contexts.text: A long walk at the end of the day is the most relaxing thing I do.
The hotel was quiet and relaxing, exactly what we needed.
Activities that people find relaxing vary considerably between age groups.

confusables.difference: Relaxing is the cause; relaxed is the effect on you.
Restful is quieter and more literary; relaxing is the everyday word.

entry_json.avoid: Never write 'I am relaxing' when you mean 'I am relaxed'. The -ing form as an adjective describes the thing, not the person.

entry_json.definition: to allow someone or something to leave or escape, or to make information or a product available
entry_json.own_context_sentence: The factory releases treated water back into the river.
example_sentences: The band released their first album in 2019.
He was released from hospital after two nights.

contexts.text: The factory releases treated water back into the river downstream.
They released the album about three years ago and I still listen to it.
The government released the figures only after repeated requests.

confusables.difference: Publish is used for books, articles and reports. Release is used for films, music, products and official data.
Free as a verb is used for people trapped or imprisoned; release is more formal and also works for information.

entry_json.avoid: The s is pronounced /s/, not /z/: ri-LEESE.

entry_json.definition: closely connected with the subject being discussed, and therefore important to it
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Only evidence that is directly relevant to the question should be included.
example_sentences: Please attach any relevant documents.
That point is interesting, but it is not relevant here.

contexts.text: Only evidence directly relevant to the question should be included in the answer.
That's interesting, but I'm not sure it's relevant to what we're deciding.
Please attach any relevant documents to support your application.

confusables.difference: Related just means connected. Relevant means the connection actually matters to the point being made.
Important judges value in general; relevant judges usefulness to this particular question.

entry_json.avoid: 'Relevant to', never 'relevant for' or 'relevant with'. In IELTS, going off topic means losing Task Response marks.

entry_json.definition: able to be trusted to do what is expected, or to be accurate
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Public transport here is cheap but not reliable.
example_sentences: We need reliable data before drawing any conclusion.
He is the most reliable person on the team.

contexts.text: Public transport in the city is cheap but not especially reliable.
My old car wasn't reliable at all, so I finally gave up on it.
Reliable data is needed before any firm conclusion can be drawn.

confusables.difference: Trustworthy is about honesty and character. Reliable is about consistent performance, and applies to machines and services too.
Dependable is a close synonym used mainly of people; reliable is broader.

entry_json.avoid: The opposite is 'unreliable', not 'non-reliable'.

entry_json.definition: the feeling of happiness when something unpleasant stops or does not happen, or help given to people in need
entry_json.own_context_sentence: It was a relief to discover the deadline had been extended.
example_sentences: Aid agencies provided emergency relief within days.
Paracetamol offers short-term relief from the pain.

contexts.text: It was an enormous relief to discover that the deadline had been extended.
Aid agencies provided emergency relief within days of the earthquake.
The medication offers only short-term relief from the symptoms.

confusables.difference: Relief is the noun with an f. Relieve is the verb with a v. The spelling change catches many learners.
Comfort is ongoing physical or emotional ease; relief is the moment when something bad ends.

entry_json.avoid: 'What a relief!' is a natural exclamation in speech but too informal for an essay.

entry_json.definition: the belief in and worship of a god or gods, or a particular system of such belief
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Religion still shapes public holidays even in secular countries.
example_sentences: The school teaches about several major religions.
She does not follow any religion.

contexts.text: Religion still shapes public holidays even in largely secular countries.
Religion isn't a big part of my life, though it matters a lot to my grandparents.
The curriculum covers the beliefs and practices of several major religions.

confusables.difference: Faith is personal belief and trust. Religion is the organised system of belief and practice.
Religion is the noun, religious the adjective. Do not write 'a religion person'.

entry_json.avoid: Handle this topic carefully in Speaking. Describe practices rather than judging any belief.

entry_json.definition: connected with religion, or believing strongly in a religion
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Religious festivals remain the busiest travel periods of the year.
example_sentences: My grandmother is deeply religious.
The building was originally a religious site.

contexts.text: Religious festivals remain the busiest travel periods of the year in many countries.
My grandmother is deeply religious, but the rest of us aren't really.
The building was originally a religious site before it became a museum.

confusables.difference: Spiritual describes inner belief that need not belong to any organised religion. Religious implies a specific faith and its practices.
Religious is the adjective; religion is the noun. 'Religious' cannot be the subject of a sentence.

entry_json.avoid: Note the spelling: reli-gious, with -gious at the end, not -geous.

entry_json.definition: to need or depend on someone or something in order to work or survive
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Rural communities still rely heavily on the bus service.
example_sentences: Many households rely on a single income.
You cannot rely on the figures without checking the source.

contexts.text: Rural communities still rely heavily on a bus service that is being cut back.
I rely on my phone for absolutely everything, which is probably unhealthy.
Many households now rely on a single income to cover rising costs.

confusables.difference: Almost identical in meaning. 'Depend on' is slightly more common in speech; 'rely on' emphasises trust that it will work.
minimal_pair: We rely on the weather forecast.

confusables.difference: Trust is about belief in honesty; rely is about needing something to function.

entry_json.avoid: Always 'rely on' or 'rely upon'. Never 'rely to' or 'rely in'.

entry_json.definition: to stay in the same place or condition, or to be left after everything else has gone
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Unemployment remains the biggest concern for people in the region.
example_sentences: Only two of the original buildings remain.
The cause of the fault remains unclear.

contexts.text: Unemployment remains the single biggest concern for people in the region.
Only two of the original buildings remain, which is a shame.
The cause of the fault remains unclear despite two investigations.

confusables.difference: Stay is the everyday word, especially about people in places. Remain is formal and is the natural verb for figures and conditions.
The rest is a noun for what is left; remain is the verb.

entry_json.avoid: Remain is not used in the continuous. Write 'The problem remains', not 'is remaining'.

entry_json.definition: something that someone says, expressing an opinion or observation
entry_json.own_context_sentence: His remark about immigration was widely criticised.
example_sentences: She made a passing remark about the cost.
The report closes with a few general remarks.

contexts.text: His remark about immigration was widely criticised in the following days.
She made a passing remark about the cost, and I've thought about it since.
The report closes with a few general remarks about future research.

confusables.difference: Comment is the more common word and is often invited. A remark is spontaneous and may be casual or pointed.
A statement is formal and prepared; a remark is brief and often unplanned.

entry_json.avoid: You 'make a remark', not 'say a remark'.

entry_json.definition: to make someone remember something they must do, or to make them think of something
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Please remind me to send the form before Friday.
example_sentences: The photograph reminds me of my first year here.
Staff are reminded that the building closes at ten.

contexts.text: Please remind me to send the form before Friday.
Staff are reminded that the building closes at ten each evening.
The findings remind us that correlation does not establish causation.

confusables.difference: You remember something yourself. You remind someone else. The subject is different.
minimal_pair: She reminded me of the date.

confusables.difference: 'Remind me of' brings a memory back. 'Remind me to' prompts a future action.

entry_json.avoid: Remind needs a person as its object: 'remind me', not 'remind that the meeting is at three' with no object.

entry_json.definition: far away from towns and people, or done from a distance using technology
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Delivering healthcare to remote villages remains expensive.
example_sentences: The job is fully remote, so I can live anywhere.
There is only a remote chance of that happening.

contexts.text: Delivering healthcare to remote villages remains prohibitively expensive.
My job is fully remote now, so I only go in about once a month.
Remote working has changed demand for office space in city centres.

confusables.difference: Distant states physical or emotional distance. Remote adds the idea of being hard to reach and cut off.
Rural means countryside, which may still be well connected. Remote means isolated.

entry_json.avoid: 'A remote chance' means a very small one. Do not confuse it with the physical sense.

entry_json.definition: money paid regularly for the use of a house, flat or room
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Rent takes up more than half my monthly income.
example_sentences: Rents in the city have risen faster than wages.
The rent includes water but not electricity.

contexts.text: Rent now takes up more than half of my monthly income.
Rents in the city have risen considerably faster than average wages.
I am writing to query the rent increase notified in your letter of 2 April.

confusables.difference: In British English you rent a home for a long period and hire a car or equipment for a short one.
minimal_pair: hire a car for the weekend

confusables.difference: A mortgage is a loan used to buy a home; rent is money paid to a landlord for using one.

entry_json.avoid: Rent as a noun is usually uncountable for one property: 'the rent is £900', not 'the rents are'.

entry_json.definition: happening or done many times
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Repeated failures to fix the problem have damaged public trust.
example_sentences: Despite repeated requests, no reply was received.
Repeated exposure to loud noise damages hearing.

contexts.text: Repeated failures to fix the problem have damaged public trust in the service.
Despite repeated requests, I have received no reply to my complaint.
I made repeated attempts to contact them and eventually gave up.

confusables.difference: Frequent describes how often something happens over time. Repeated stresses that the same thing happened again and again.
Continuous means without stopping; repeated means happening over and over with gaps.

entry_json.avoid: Repeated goes before the noun. Do not write 'The requests were repeated many times' when 'repeated requests' is shorter and stronger.

entry_json.definition: to act or speak officially for someone, or to be a sign or symbol of something
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Each column represents one year of data.
example_sentences: She was elected to represent the students on the committee.
This figure represents a five per cent rise.

contexts.text: Each column in the chart represents one year of recorded data.
I was elected to represent our year on the student committee.
The organisation represents the interests of tenants in the private sector.

confusables.difference: Stand for is the informal equivalent for symbols and abbreviations. Represent is formal and covers both meanings.
Present means show or give; represent means act on behalf of, or symbolise.

entry_json.avoid: In Task 1, use 'represents' for what a bar or line shows. Do not write 'represents about', which is redundant.

entry_json.definition: a person chosen to act or speak for a group of people
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Each department sends one representative to the monthly meeting.
example_sentences: A union representative attended the hearing.
The sample was not representative of the wider population.

contexts.text: Each department sends one representative to the monthly meeting.
There was a student representative on the panel, which made a difference.
The sample was not representative of the wider population, which limits the findings.

confusables.difference: A delegate is sent to one particular conference or meeting. A representative holds the role over time.
As an adjective it means typical of a larger group: 'a representative sample'. This is the key research use.

entry_json.avoid: Watch the stress: rep-ri-ZEN-ta-tiv. It is a long word and mispronouncing it is very audible.

entry_json.definition: the opinion that people generally have about someone or something
entry_json.own_context_sentence: The university has built a strong reputation for research.
example_sentences: The city has a reputation for being expensive.
One serious mistake can destroy a reputation built over decades.

contexts.text: The university has built a strong international reputation for medical research.
The city has a reputation for being expensive, which is fairly deserved.
One serious error can destroy a reputation built over several decades.

confusables.difference: Fame is being widely known. Reputation is what people think of you, and can be good or bad.
minimal_pair: He has a reputation for honesty.

confusables.difference: Image is how something is deliberately presented; reputation is what people actually conclude.

entry_json.avoid: 'A reputation for' takes a noun or -ing: 'a reputation for being late', not 'a reputation to be late'.

entry_json.definition: to need something, or to make something necessary by rule
entry_json.own_context_sentence: The role requires at least two years of relevant experience.
example_sentences: All passengers are required to show identification.
Reducing emissions will require action from every sector.

contexts.text: The role requires at least two years of directly relevant experience.
It required a lot more effort than I expected, honestly.
Reducing emissions on this scale will require coordinated action from every sector.

confusables.difference: Need is the everyday word and can be used about people directly. Require is formal and is standard for rules and job descriptions.
minimal_pair: Applicants are required to submit two references.

confusables.difference: Request means politely ask for; require means make necessary or demand.

entry_json.avoid: Require is not used in the continuous: 'The job requires', not 'is requiring'.

entry_json.definition: something that is needed or that must be done because of a rule
entry_json.own_context_sentence: Meeting the language requirement is the last step for most applicants.
example_sentences: The course has no formal entry requirements.
Safety requirements have become considerably stricter.

contexts.text: Meeting the language requirement is the final step for most international applicants.
The entry requirements weren't as high as I'd feared, luckily.
Please confirm that the property meets all current safety requirements.
